#6012. China’s Economics of Denial

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

Oliver Melton is a Director with Rhodium Group’s China practice.

Logan Wright is a Partner at Rhodium Group and leads its research on China’s economy and financial markets. He is the author of the book Broken China: How the Economic Miracle Shattered and What it Means for the World.

Beijing’s Theory of Success in the Face of Failure

China has correctly diagnosed its most pressing economic problems. The Chinese Communist Party has acknowledged that its economy relies too much on investment and exports and that persistently weak household consumption is the core threat to future growth. The leadership also knows that this imbalanced growth model is causing trade friction with developed and emerging economies alike and will continue to do so. They know there is a growing chorus of economists (including many quiet voices in China) raising the alarm that, if Beijing does not make major changes soon, China will face ever-slower growth, cascading trade disputes, and potentially stagnating household income.

But what is puzzling is that the country’s leaders are not acting. Beijing has announced only modest plans to boost household consumption and domestic demand, and its overall economic strategy remains essentially unchanged—focused on expanding investment in manufacturing, especially in advanced technologies and new strategic industries.

Theories abound as to why Beijing has chosen to ignore the warnings. Many speculate that Chinese leader Xi Jinping is not receiving accurate information or that he and his closest allies have abandoned development as a priority in favor of national security goals or a desire to control the commanding heights of global industry. Others argue that Beijing knows what it should do, but political or institutional constraints prevent it from taking decisive action.

In truth, while these factors all play a part in shaping policy, the real explanation is far simpler. The party is sticking to this path because the leadership believes it is working. It sees the same troubling data—including rising external surpluses, weak consumption, slower household income growth, weak credit demand, rising unemployment and underemployment, and persistent deflation—but it has reached wildly different conclusions about what these developments indicate and what Beijing should do in response.

Chinese economic policy is nested within a methodical planning process, which is meant to ensure that short-term pressures do not distract from long-term priorities. The problem is that the long-term strategy is predicated on the belief that control of advanced technologies and industry will trigger a new round of high-speed growth. This economic strategy can best be understood as a Marxism-infused misapplication of neoclassical economic development theory: Beijing is obsessed with control over technology and physical capital and believes that its ultrahigh levels of investment will accelerate productivity gains and wage growth. But a disproportionate focus on manufacturing and technology cannot increase productivity or wages if those investments are decoupled from the needs of the market and trends in aggregate final demand. This is especially true in a country as large as China—already the world’s largest exporter—that cannot rely on further exports to fuel growth.

China’s worldview treats development as equivalent to capital accumulation and sees productivity as determined by the control and deployment of technology. It posits that the growth of the service sector, higher wages, and higher consumption are the consequences of that physical underlying foundation—they follow naturally in later stages of the development process once the productive industries have flourished. In this conception of economic development, the right strategy is always more investment, more industry, and more technology. The role of the state is to ensure that household savings and industrial profits are recycled through the state-owned banking system or government-guided capital into priority investments rather than frivolous activities, such as services or consumption. The resulting structural imbalance that weakens household income growth, the service sector, and public services was thus not an accident; in China’s economic development theory, this is seen as self-discipline that will pay off with more rapid long-term development.

A key corollary to this view is that the government’s macroeconomic management must guide resource allocation proactively through hands-on intervention, not impassively through interest rates and exchange rates. The state can harness the dynamism and ambition of markets to promote efficiency and innovation in defined spaces, but it is the government’s job to identify the correct focal points for investment to ensure that priority sectors grow at maximum speed and then to intervene to ameliorate imbalances when they inevitably arise.

In this conception of macroeconomics, the economy consists of a massive input-output table where every cell in the matrix is a sector that consumes other cells’ outputs and provides inputs to other producers. If there is an imbalance in supply or demand for certain products—which becomes evident in high or low prices—it may be because of overinvestment in the producing sector or underinvestment in downstream consuming sectors. Government policy seeks to increase output and steadily lower prices by facilitating investment and production throughout the matrix, adjusting the pace and balance of resource allocation as needed if one cell’s output exceeds the demands of the others. The goal is not to develop overcapacity or low profitability in these targeted sectors, but the optimal path for rapid development will inevitably push sectors in that direction.

Beijing has followed this playbook closely. When, for instance, the real estate sector collapsed in 2022 and the structural imbalances in China’s economy became too big to ignore, Beijing responded by increasing its efforts to micromanage credit flows, reversing experiments with interest rate liberalization and financial market reforms while tightening oversight of capital markets and industrial policy funding. Central bank relending facilities now channel low-cost bank loans to prioritize industrial upgrading and equipment purchases for targeted sectors. Thousands of government-run equity funds provide low-cost capital to firms that support a web of industrial and technology strategies. State-owned enterprises intervene to help boost valuations in the stock market, and regulators prioritize firms in strategic sectors for new listings. When a sector is overinvested, policy campaigns such as “anti-involution”—a neologism that describes a basket of discordant policies to resolve overcapacity—are deployed to slow future investment, buttress profitability by fixing prices, or set standards to restrict market entry in a bid to slow output while the other cells in the input-output tables catch up and restore balance over time.

Although hard to comprehend in the context of a market economy, some aspects of this approach have an understandable internal logic in China, especially at a micro level. The collapse of the property sector—roughly a quarter of GDP at its peak—sent massive shock waves through very specific supply and demand pathways in the economy. It made sense for Beijing to calibrate policy for the affected sectors and think in terms of input-output tables as it designed its responses. The frequency of bubbles in China’s equity, commodity, and property markets over the past 15 years has left policymakers deeply wary of accommodative monetary policy for the entire economy, which helps explain why they are experimenting with more targeted tools aimed at specific sectors.

Likewise, a certain level of triumphalism in Beijing is understandable, given that Chinese companies are breaking into pole positions in major conventional industries, such as autos and telecommunications, and many others are poised to thrive in cutting-edge sectors, such as robotics and biotechnology—all in the wake of a massive hit to GDP. For a generation of economic policymakers who cut their teeth trying to revitalize a moribund planned economy in the 1990s and the first decade of this century, the emergence of world-leading (often private) firms is definitive evidence that Beijing has found a winning recipe. From this perspective, Beijing is also dismissive of foreign complaints about unfair market interventions or trade imbalances as the sour grapes of rich countries that had grown accustomed to rent-seeking technology monopolies.

China’s leaders also see some deflation as the fruits of hard-won efficiency gains: the elimination of bottlenecks, economies of scale in manufacturing clusters, construction of world-class infrastructure, improved logistics, and removal of market barriers that have lowered costs up and down manufacturing supply chains. One-off cost reductions from efficiency gains or the abrupt loss of construction activity must be digested by the economy, they would argue, not offset by stimulus. And while foreign commentators and dignitaries warn of growing trade pushback, the data tells a surprisingly different story: China’s export growth barely slowed as the Trump administration imposed sweeping duties and the European Union set up defenses against a handful of sectors, such as electric vehicles.

The core problem with China’s economic strategy, however, is that aggregate domestic demand consistently falls far short of domestic supply. Chinese planners’ input-output tables will not balance unless domestic workers are buying the goods that China’s industries produce. Otherwise, everything else must be exported, often at lower prices. The leadership understands this in principle but believes that the control of advanced industries and technology will, ipso facto, cause productivity to rise, sustain economic growth into the future, and generate higher wages and therefore higher consumption.

This is the flaw in Beijing’s approach—the dangerous legacy of vestigial Marxism and misapplied neoclassical growth theory. In reality, state intervention in markets can depress overall productivity and workers can see flat wages even when China succeeds at promoting advanced industries.

It is true that capital and technology create productivity gains in well-functioning market economies. But the causality usually breaks down if resources are allocated by policy interventions that are divorced from returns on investment. The control or ownership of advanced industries does not inherently cause economic growth, because they are far too small a share of the economy. Instead, new products or technologies generate productivity when they are distributed and used throughout the economy in ways that improve efficiency or increase output. It is not the success of a robotics firm that leads to efficiency gains, for example, it is the deployment of its robots in factories to save production costs—namely by displacing workers—and boost output. If those benefits do not exceed the true cost of the new industrial robots—even with layers of subsidies—then the net effect is not positive, no matter how impressive the factories themselves are, or how successful the robotics firm itself appears.

The use of new production technologies also requires a degree of creative destruction that Beijing’s own industrial policy interventions have inhibited. When governments, not price-conscious firms, make technology and investment decisions, policymakers are not just gambling that they know better than the market how to boost long-run performance. They are also betting that they know how to use those technologies to create innovative new business models. Yet in China, state influence over resource allocation has ossified markets, especially by reducing bankruptcies, in ways that limit the fruits of innovation and efficiency gains in the broader economy. Additionally, much of China’s industrial policy aims to build self-reliance, which, by definition, focuses on duplicative investments that buttress domestic industrial prowess without necessarily adding efficiency.

Moreover, even though China’s many layers of industrial policy have helped launch successful companies and built an impressive fleet of ultramodern factories, there are also tremendous inefficiencies and waste that never make the headlines. Overall productivity must be calculated comprehensively, evaluating the net output gains against all the industrial subsidies, bad debts, foregone profits, and indirect support for investment that the government has provided. The reality is that China’s aggregate success rate is far lower than the shining stars would suggest: the remarkable global reach of electric vehicle and battery makers such as BYD, CATL, and Li Auto masks the dozens of failed companies that generated nonperforming loans and ate up unprofitable capital subsidies throughout the bulk of the sector and its supply chain. It is far from obvious that the net return on investment from industrial policy spending, estimated by the International Monetary Fund to be up to four percent of GDP, is positive, and it could be deeply negative, despite pockets of success.

Finally, Beijing is betting that superefficient manufacturing and success in strategic industries will eventually lead to higher wages, which will then cause consumption to surge. It is true that productivity growth causes real incomes to rise in a competitive market economy. But if investments in labor-saving technologies are driven by state policy, not returns on investment, wages can fall even as firms become more efficient. Rising household income requires a key intermediate step: employment, which is not a core characteristic of China’s capital-intensive, advanced manufacturing investment strategy. Indeed, state funding has helped China—a middle-income economy—become a world leader in high-tech “dark factories” that operate without distracting human accommodations, such as light. This may increase output in prized manufacturing cells in the input-output tables, but if demand for labor is not growing in aggregate, the whole equation starts to fall apart.

Still, the most pernicious consequence of Beijing’s economic model is entrenched deflation. The focus on expanding production combined with China’s weak consumer demand has caused the producer price index to fall for longer than it has risen over the past decade. This is a far larger threat to China’s economy than a mere nuisance of sectoral imbalances. Deflation reduces private-sector credit demand; undercuts incentives for new investments; and crushes employment, wage expectations, and, therefore, consumer confidence, which leads to weaker domestic demand—not in carefully demarcated input-output relationships but throughout the economy. Deflation also saps fiscal revenues and puts pressure on financial institutions in ways that severely limit the state’s capacity to act decisively the longer it lasts. Deflationary pressures in China also spill over to the global economy through cheaper exports and a weakening real exchange rate, driving more tensions between Beijing and its trading partners.

There is immense risk in falling behind the curve in fighting deflation, but Beijing is not likely to change course if it continues to believe its strategy will boost productivity and jumpstart domestic demand in the long run. Some analysts speculate that Beijing could be forced into a reappraisal of its vision in response to unemployment pressures or the proliferation of foreign trade friction, but it has already shown its cards. The accumulation of unemployment, underemployment, and low wages for Chinese households and workers are already significant, yet Beijing has responded with only modest new household subsidies and incremental investment in social services. Likewise, as external trade tensions have risen, Beijing has managed these country-by-country disputes as diplomatic issues, through a mix of threats and negotiations, to preserve the bulk of China’s export markets.

The decision to pursue short-term Band-Aid measures for a weak labor market and foreign trade tensions is confusing at first pass. For a government laser-focused on self-reliance and eliminating foreign dependencies, it is a curious strategy to become ever more dependent on foreign demand—over which Beijing has little control—as its primary driver of economic growth. Likewise, for a regime that is obsessed with social stability, it would seem prudent to focus more on wages and labor demand. Yet the strategy makes a degree of sense when viewed from the leadership’s perspective that China is in a transitional period. It may be unpleasant and difficult, but it is an unavoidable step on the path to a technology-led growth model.

The leadership’s current confidence in this transition process means that it could be many years before the warning signs, already visible, become persuasive internally. This all but guarantees that Beijing will continue to defer action while deflationary pressures and external trade tensions build. Deflation and weak corporate profitability are already eroding China’s fiscal revenues, which have basically been flat in nominal terms since 2019. Deflation and the growing debt burden are also corroding the financial system, which will ultimately require large write-offs and recapitalization from the government budget to prevent credit growth from slowing further. A $54 billion bank recapitalization just took place two months ago, with little effect on lending.

Beijing’s ideological commitment to its industry- and technology-focused development strategy is creating a dangerous cycle that will likely produce weaker consumption, slower income growth, and even greater trade friction with the rest of the world. Moreover, in the face of such challenges, China’s economic leadership is compensating by expanding state intervention in the economy in ways that further undermine market forces and the independence of the private sector. At this rate, even if the leadership eventually recognizes the need to change strategy, China may not have the fiscal or financial space to rebalance the economy toward a more sustainable and diversified growth model.

#6010. Democrat Cindy Holscher wins Kansas governor's race, extending party's hold on governor's mansion

Kansas elected Democrat Cindy Holscher as governor, marking the party's third consecutive gubernatorial victory despite the state's Republican presidential streak.

Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher won the Kansas governor’s race, defeating Republican Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson in the open contest to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, The Associated Press projected.The victory keeps the governor’s mansion in Democratic hands and marks the third consecutive Kansas gubernatorial election won by a Democrat. Kelly won the office in 2018 and secured a second term in 2022.

The result underscores Democrats’ continued success in Kansas gubernatorial races despite Republicans’ longstanding dominance in the state’s presidential elections. The GOP has carried Kansas in every presidential election since 1968.

GOP WIPEOUT GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE AS DEMS QUIETLY SCORE ANOTHER MAJOR WIN WITH BIG RAMIFICATIONS

Kansas Gov.-elect Cindy Holscher, a Democrat, campaigns in Lenexa on Nov. 2, 2026, ahead of her victory over Republican Ty Masterson.  (Nick Oxford/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Holscher has served in the Kansas Senate since 2021 after previously spending four years in the state House. She secured the Democratic nomination after defeating fellow state Sen. Ethan Corson, who was endorsed by Kelly and former Democratic Gov. Kathleen Sebelius, in the August primary.Holscher faced scrutiny during the campaign over resurfaced social media posts from 2023 in which she suggested Jesus Christ could have been transgender. The comments came during a debate over proposed Kansas legislation restricting drag performances in front of children.

Holscher celebrated her victory in a post on X, thanking Kansas voters as she prepared to take office.

Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher will become Kansas’ next governor after defeating Republican Ty Masterson in the Nov. 3 election, The Associated Press projected Thursday. (REUTERS)

THE TOP TRUMP OFFICIALS DEMOCRATS ADMIT ARE ON THEIR HIT LIST FOR INVESTIGATIONS IN THE NEW CONGRESS

"Thank you, Kansas! It’s the honor of a lifetime to serve as your next Governor," Holscher wrote.

Masterson, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump in the crowded GOP primary, conceded the race in a post on X and said he had called Holscher to congratulate her.

"It looks like we will come up just short, but the things we fought for are no less important today than they were yesterday."

Masterson, who has served as Kansas Senate president since 2021, also pointed to Republicans' continued control of the state Legislature and said he would return to the Senate in January to focus on property taxes, public safety, affordability and schools.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

World Brief: Hoax Bomb Threats Target Hundreds of European Schools

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at more hoax bomb threats across Europe, the status of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and Spain’s housing affordability crisis.

False bomb threats once again disrupted thousands of Europeans on Wednesday in what officials and experts suspect may be part of an ongoing campaign of hybrid warfare against the continent. But rather than affecting airline passengers, this time, the threats targeted students.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at more hoax bomb threats across Europe, the status of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and Spain’s housing affordability crisis.

False bomb threats once again disrupted thousands of Europeans on Wednesday in what officials and experts suspect may be part of an ongoing campaign of hybrid warfare against the continent. But rather than affecting airline passengers, this time, the threats targeted students.

Around 6,300 schools across Italy received anonymous bomb threats on Wednesday, forcing hundreds of institutions to evacuate their classrooms. Schools in Scotland, Ireland, and Northern Ireland also received such warnings, though those emails were quickly classified as hoaxes and therefore did not disrupt learning.

The incident prompted Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to convene an emergency cabinet meeting on Wednesday with cybersecurity experts to discuss next steps. “The reports appear to be part of a strategy aimed at causing alarm and concern, which is currently being investigated in depth,” Meloni posted on social media, adding that there is no evidence to suggest that the threats pose a concrete danger.

It is unclear who was responsible for Wednesday’s scare, though at least one email to an Italian school was reportedly signed by a “Mikhail Andropov,” the same purported author of last week’s bomb threats against newsrooms in Bulgaria and Ireland.

At least 21 European nations have experienced similar hoaxes or actual cyberattacks in the past few weeks. That includes false bomb threats on at least 27 different European airlines, hacking operations on supermarket refrigeration systems, and coordinated cyberattacks on blood banks. These incidents have disrupted air traffic for thousands of travelers, spoiled food, sparked fires, and threatened critical healthcare infrastructure.

“We obviously need to be vigilant,” Italian Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara told local media on Wednesday. “But we must also be aware that in a context where hybrid warfare is increasingly being used as a tool to destabilize nations and economies, we need to prepare ourselves.”

Some security officials suspect that Russia could be to blame, arguing that the recent slew of incidents may be targeting European countries that have armed or financed Ukraine. In recent months, Moscow has been accused of ramping up hybrid warfare operations in Europe, from a failed drone attack on Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport in August to repeated incursions into Denmark, Estonia, Lithuania, Poland, and Romania. Russia continues to deny any involvement in the incidents.

The Kremlin, however, isn’t the only suspect. On Monday, French authorities accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind last month’s supermarket refrigeration attack, and the following day, the country’s foreign ministry summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris.

“We rule nothing out and will take all measures, including those we may not disclose publicly, that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Tuesday. Such measures could include new European Union sanctions on Tehran.

Little peace progress. Russia and Ukraine ended two days of U.S.-mediated peace talks on Wednesday with an agreement to exchange prisoners in the next few weeks. According to U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner, this will be the “biggest humanitarian release of prisoners” thus far, though exact numbers will not be finalized until Thursday.

However, the swap agreement was one of the only breakthroughs to emerge out of the talks in Abu Dhabi. Both sides remain bogged down by old sticking points, such as whether to impose a temporary cease-fire before a permanent truce and if Ukraine should relinquish Russian-occupied territory in the Donbas region.

The lack of a European presence in Abu Dhabi may also have hindered the conference’s progress; Moscow does not want any European involvement in direct negotiations, but both Kyiv and Washington wish to add them to future talks. “We believe that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky posted on X on Wednesday.

But this week’s diplomatic efforts aren’t over yet. On Thursday, Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff will head to Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin before traveling to Dublin for similar talks with Zelensky.

Housing reform. Millions of Spanish residents took part in a general strike on Wednesday to protest the country’s housing affordability crisis. Backed by Spain’s two largest trade unions, the nationwide demonstrations are the first of their kind in 14 years and could help Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez steer the conversation back in his favor ahead of snap parliamentary elections later this month.

Spain’s housing reckoning kicked off in September, when an 87-year-old Madrid resident was forcibly evicted from her home. Her struggle became the symbol of a wider conversation over skyrocketing rents, stagnant wages, and weak tenant protections across the country. Sánchez’s efforts to enact stronger tenant rights were blocked by opposition parties, though, prompting the left-wing leader to call for a snap vote.

However, any political momentum that Sánchez earned from pursuing housing reform has come under threat in the wake of last month’s deadly train crash, which killed at least 69 people and injured more than 100 others. It was the country’s second deadly high-speed rail incident this year, raising questions about insufficient government oversight and maintenance. Sánchez’s administration is therefore likely hoping that Wednesday’s strike puts the public’s focus back on housing concerns before Spaniards head to the polls on Nov. 29.

The nuclear status quo. Iran vowed again on Wednesday not to allow any enriched nuclear material to leave its territory, prompting global oil prices to rise after a short-term reprieve. The declaration echoes a similar directive issued by Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei in May; however, Tehran reiterating the stance now could hinder efforts to restart U.S.-Iran peace talks, which largely hinge on the future of Tehran’s nuclear program.

The White House has insisted that any final deal with Tehran must involve Iran surrendering its stockpile of highly enriched uranium and accepting curbs on its nuclear program. “Crazy Islamists in Tehran will never, ever have a nuclear weapon,” U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Tuesday in a defiant address defending the Trump administration’s controversial handling of the Iran war.

Iran maintains that it does not seek a nuclear weapon and that it has the right to enrich uranium for civilian use. “We need the ​enriched material to design ships and submarines that work on nuclear energy,” Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Wednesday. However, the International Atomic Energy Agency estimated that before the United States and Israel attacked Iran’s nuclear facilities in June 2025, Iran had 440 kg of uranium enriched to 60 percent—a level far higher than what is needed for civilian purposes. How much highly enriched uranium the country still has today is not clear.

Rezaei’s statement rattled energy markets, with both Brent and West Texas Intermediate futures rising 1.3 percent. In recent weeks, global oil prices dropped considerably amid hopes that the war will end soon, particularly after Trump appeared to rule out launching a fresh wave of strikes for now.

Formal business attire may be the standard for most Japanese lawmakers, but one legislator is proving to be the exception. Last month, professional wrestler Billy Ken Kid was elected to the city of Kawanishi’s municipal assembly. Not wanting to leave his old identity behind, Billy asked city council members to approve him wearing one of his iconic wrestling masks during sessions. On Friday, the chamber greenlit Billy’s request in a “dream … come true” for the 52-year-old. However, the new lawmaker has agreed to keep his identity uninhibited when attending ceremonies outside of the assembly hall, such as memorial services.

Alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp

#6008. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

#6007. The New Congress Can Repair Civil-Military Relations

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

PETER D. FEAVER is Professor of Political Science and Public Policy at Duke University and the author of Thanks for Your Service: The Causes and Consequences of Public Confidence in the U.S. Military.

HEIDI URBEN is Professor of the Practice and Associate Director of Georgetown University’s Center for Security Studies in the Walsh School of Foreign Service.

How It Can Reclaim Its Constitutional Powers

Article I of the Constitution gives Congress sweeping powers to raise, maintain, and equip the armed forces. But the current Congress has done little to use these powers. The intense, frenetic activity of the past two years has undone established norms for military professionalism and may shape civil-military relations for a generation. Yet it has been led almost entirely by the executive branch with little meaningful involvement or pushback from Capitol Hill.

The next Congress will face great pressure to reverse course and in doing so could shore up the historical norms of American civil-military relations. The concern today is not a military that is defying civilians—the traditional bogeyman of American political leaders since the founding of the Republic. Rather, the fear is that the thousands of changes, large and small, that the executive branch has so rapidly imposed on the military may end up undermining the professional ethic on which the U.S. form of civilian control depends.

The incoming Congress can push U.S. civil-military relations in a healthier direction by overseeing the executive branch more actively than its predecessor. It can also help restore trust with both the military and the American public if it focuses on providing greater transparency, takes a more assertive role in conducting defense policy, reinforces the military’s nonpartisan professional ethic, and establishes a new bipartisan commission to reinvigorate the military profession. Congress has the power and authority to improve civil-military relations. The new session, starting in January, is its chance to use them before the damage becomes irreversible.

When Pete Hegseth was sworn in as defense secretary, in 2025, he had strong views on the changes he wanted to make, alleging the military had lost its warfighting focus because of misguided priorities and “wokeism.” He has pursued those changes with a zeal not seen since Robert McNamara held the office from 1961 to 1968. Hegseth has reshaped the senior officer ranks: he has fired or removed nearly two dozen senior general and flag officers, and he has gotten rid of more than one-quarter of all four-star generals, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the chiefs of the U.S. Air Force, Army, and Navy. He has fired, removed, or pulled from promotion lists approximately 80 general and flag officers, a disproportionate number of whom are women or racial minorities. Hegseth has justified those removals in the vaguest of terms, which has convinced most observers that the real reason amounts to little more than because these officers followed the lawful orders of the previous administration. No previous defense secretary has removed such large swaths of the officer corps who honored their oaths to the Constitution and faithfully implemented policies decided by their civilian superiors.

Hegseth has moved quickly, largely ignoring traditional bureaucratic practices, including rigorous staff reviews and close involvement of congressional stakeholders in changing the trajectory of the Pentagon’s policymaking and in conducting military operations. Amid ongoing questions about the legality of the boat strikes the Trump administration ordered against suspected drug traffickers last fall as well as civilian casualties in America’s war with Iran, it is critical to note that Hegseth had already fired the senior, most experienced military legal advisers—sending a warning shot across the bow of younger judge advocates—and begun a significant overhaul of the Judge Advocate General Corps. Ever since the My Lai massacre during the Vietnam War, when U.S. soldiers committed war crimes by killing hundreds of unarmed Vietnamese civilians, the JAG Corps had been empowered to help U.S. personnel abide by the laws of armed conflict. By demoting senior legal advisers and selecting less qualified personnel in those positions, however, the military’s legal voice is more marginalized today than it has been since the Vietnam War. The Trump administration has also centralized decision-making, including by placing routine actions in highly classified channels that minimize opportunities for input and deliberation.

Hegseth has done all of this—and much more—with essentially no pushback from the uniformed military or Pentagon bureaucracy. On the one hand, this shows just how strongly officers accept the principle of civilian control—a posture reinforced precisely because Hegseth has proved willing to punish even unsupported allegations of military insubordination. On the other hand, his actions have had a chilling effect across the force, creating an environment in which the military is reluctant to offer candid advice or uphold its professional standards and values when they are at odds with administration priorities. Indeed, in a highly unusual move, former government officials have publicly called for military leaders to do more to stand up to the Trump administration, even at the cost of undermining civilian control. As we argued in Foreign Affairs in 2024, however, the military cannot save democracy; only Congress and the courts can and should check presidential power.

Hegseth has enjoyed the unwavering support of President Donald Trump. But the real secret to Hegseth’s success in imposing his agenda on the Pentagon has been the unwillingness of the current Congress to exercise its Article I responsibilities or defend its traditional prerogatives. The incoming Congress can take a different approach by using its power to build trust, transparency, and accountability.

Most pressing, Congress should exercise its ability to appropriately scrutinize defense policymaking, much of which has been shrouded in secrecy under the Trump administration. The current Congress has held very few oversight hearings, and the ones that have taken place have been exchanges of insults rather than of information. When secrecy is genuinely needed, of course, Congress can issue classified briefings and hold closed hearings. But open hearings, when properly conducted, are necessary in cases in which Congress is entitled to answers, for example, about military personnel policy.

In the case of the boat strikes in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific, Congress needs to know what advice senior military commanders and their JAGs offered, and it must understand how JAG firings affect the process by which commanders discern the lawfulness of military operations. Thus far, the Defense Department has provided only superficial explanations of its actions that basically amount to “we did this because we thought it was necessary.” Such justifications fall far short of what the Constitution envisions as the best way to hold the armed forces accountable: open debate that subjects policies to rigorous scrutiny. Greater transparency would also bolster public confidence in defense policy and remove pressure on the military to have to act as a potential savior of the Constitution.

Congress should also faithfully fulfill its “advice and consent” function established in Article II, which authorizes the Senate to review and confirm presidential nominations and promotions. Hegseth’s unprecedented intervention in the meritocratic promotion process has dramatically altered the military’s upper echelons. Congress has normalized this interference, perhaps unwittingly, by approving Hegseth’s altered promotion lists with voice votes and little inquiry.

The president and the defense secretary must retain the right to remove officers in whom they have lost confidence. But Congress has the right to know why a change was made, and it needs to ensure that promotions and removals follow established law and procedures rather than ideological or partisan considerations. Because Congress created the process for meritocratic promotions, it can push the executive branch to adhere to that process. It should mandate that the defense secretary provide a written explanation, supported by documented evidence of misconduct or derogatory information, for any off-cycle removals of senior officers and restore senior officers’ promotions, which would limit unjustified removals and uphold the merit-based selection process. Improving transparency in personnel policy will have one further salutary effect: it will help retain those qualified military personnel who are wondering whether they should give up on a military career that could be derailed by politicized and capricious promotion decisions.

In addition, Congress has a responsibility to police the well-established principle and practice that the uniformed military must stay away from partisan politics. The military has largely tried to uphold this norm, even as civilian political leaders have sought to draw it into partisan debates. Each time, for instance, Hegseth attacks the Biden administration before military audiences, most of whom served during the Biden era, he unwittingly further degrades the nonpartisan ethic on which service members’ oaths of office—and thus their subordination to his own policies—depend. It sends a message that embracing partisan rhetoric is key to career advancement and signals to the public that the military is not a neutral constituency. Congress can police the executive branch’s politicization of the military through inquiries, hearings, and even measures that prohibit the use of appropriated funds for events that treat military audiences like campaign rallies. Members of Congress can also call out for censure uniformed military personnel who behave in a blatantly partisan fashion regardless of whether they support or oppose the party the member supports.

Most ambitiously, Congress should reclaim its role in making defense policy rather than only providing oversight. Legislative deference to the executive in times of war is not unique to Trump’s second term, but Congress should close loopholes that allow presidents to expand their power unchecked. If Congress wants to provide a legal justification to allow the use of force in Iran or against drug traffickers in the Caribbean or the eastern Pacific Ocean, it should do so. If it believes these actions are unlawful, however, it must use its legislative powers to constrain them. Similarly, Congress should amend the Insurrection Act to clarify and restrict the domestic use of military force. The president must retain the ability to respond to true national emergencies, but Congress should narrow the criteria for deployment of troops on U.S. soil to avoid potential abuse.

Even as it becomes more active, Congress must strenuously avoid involving the military in a partisan war. Members of Congress should not press the military to criticize the president or the defense secretary in the made-for-social-media-outrage hearings that have become commonplace in Washington. It is right and proper for Congress to ask members of the military to share their personal and professional opinions on key strategic questions. But too often, politicians try to turn officers into combatants in their partisan battles, hiding behind the armed forces to defend partisan agendas or attacking military leaders who have simply carried out the lawful orders of a president from another party. Above all, Congress should not ask the military to be a check on civilian power. Only other civilians have the authority to do that.

Congress cannot solve longer-term issues through the day-to-day legislative process. But it has other tools to more holistically improve civil-military relations and identify the most essential reforms. The time-honored strategy is to set up a nonpartisan blue-ribbon commission to analyze problems, draw attention to their importance, and recommend solutions. A national commission on the state of the professional military ethic, co-chaired by three respected individuals—one with experience in a Republican administration, one with experience in a Democratic administration, and one retired senior military leader—would have the freedom to investigate how recent developments, including attempts to politicize the military and sustain a high tempo of operations, have affected the force. At a minimum, the commission should explore impacts on recruiting and retention; professional military education, fellowships in civilian institutions, and general and flag officer development; the JAG Corps’ ability to provide commanders with candid, independent legal advice; and the state of the National Guard.

The current Congress has not shown enough interest in exercising its own powers. The next one can make a clean break and rediscover the body’s ability to carry out the functions that are necessary to improve civil-military relations. The new Congress can demonstrate its commitment to fulfilling its responsibilities by providing ordinary legislative oversight in the raising, maintaining, and equipping of the armed forces. And on thorny issues that require a bigger response, Congress can start the reform process by creating a national commission to lay out an agenda for action. Even after two years of enormous strain that has eroded best practices in civil-military relations, the next Congress is well positioned to reverse the slide and shore up Americans’ faith in a nonpartisan, professional military that is essential to democracy.

#6006. Van Hollen challenges Schumer for Senate leadership after Democratic election sweep

Several newly-elected Democratic senators suggest they are not committed to supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader. Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the Democratic Party’s priorities and leadership plans as Congress prepares to return to session.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., officially has a challenger for the mantle of Democratic leader, and incoming majority leader, in the Senate.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has become a progressive darling and outlet for those against Schumer’s bid for another term as top Democrat, officially announced that he was jumping in to challenge the longtime figurehead of the Senate Democratic Caucus.

"In this election, the American people called for change," Van Hollen said in a statement. "They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies – but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people."

BERNIE SANDERS SAYS HE WON'T BACK SCHUMER AS PUSH FOR NEW LEADERSHIP GAINS STEAM

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, speaks during a news conference following a Maryland delegation meeting at the U.S. Capitol in Washington on Thursday, June 25, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," he continued. "This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader."

Van Hollen, 67, has served in Congress for 23 years, first starting in the House before moving to the Senate in 2017. Schumer, 75, has been an elected official since 1981.

The Maryland Democrat’s decision to run against Schumer comes after a listening tour with Senate Democrats and follows his initial ambition of "kicking the tires" on jumping into the 2028 presidential conversation.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: A USER’S MANUAL TO UPCOMING LEADERSHIP ELECTIONS IN THE HOUSE AND SENATE

Since entering the Senate, Van Hollen has occupied Schumer’s left flank. It wasn’t until earlier this week that he fully took a shot at him, arguing that the longtime leader had chosen the "crypto industry" and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) over progressive candidates that eventually won during this past midterm cycle.

But he's managed to capture some of the superstars of the left, most notably Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who pushed Van Hollen to run.

"The American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism. But we have yet to earn our mandate. That will require bold leadership. I called on Sen. [Chris Van Hollen] to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority."

RACHEL MADDOW WELCOMES 'BIG FIGHT' BETWEEN SOCIALIST AND MODERATE DEMOCRATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee headquarters on Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Tom Brenner/Getty Images)

Schumer did not take the challenge lying down.

"I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead," Schumer said on X. "I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader."

"I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people," he continued.Neither did his allies. Schumer has maintained since Democrats flipped the Senate that he would be the one to lead them over the next two years. And one of his possible lieutenants, Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who is vying to replace Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., as Democratic whip, is riding with him through the storm. "Senate Democrats had historic victories last week, thanks to our talented candidates and the hard work of our caucus, led by Senator Schumer. And it was not the first time he has led this caucus back to the majority," Schatz said in a statement.

"The American people sent a clear message: they want us to lower costs, end a needless war, and fight corruption. Our caucus has the right to have a conversation about the path ahead, but we have no time to waste," he continued. "We must move quickly to vote, unify, and get to work. I endorse Senator Schumer for leader and will be voting for him in the caucus election."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

#6003. How Democrats Will Wield Power on Foreign Policy

When Democrats take over the U.S. House and Senate in January, how will they use their new powers, and what foreign-policy issues will they prioritize? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Jason Crow, a former Army Ranger who served multiple tours in Iraq and Afghanistan and won reelection as a Democrat from Colorado’s 6th Congressional District. Crow helped lead the party’s efforts to select a diverse slate of candidates across the country, and he also helped direct their battleground and campaign strategy. He serves on the House Armed Services and Intelligence committees.

The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

When Democrats take over the U.S. House and Senate in January, how will they use their new powers, and what foreign-policy issues will they prioritize? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Jason Crow, a former Army Ranger who served multiple tours in Iraq and Afghanistan and won reelection as a Democrat from Colorado’s 6th Congressional District. Crow helped lead the party’s efforts to select a diverse slate of candidates across the country, and he also helped direct their battleground and campaign strategy. He serves on the House Armed Services and Intelligence committees.

The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Ravi Agrawal: I want to start with how you’re interpreting last week’s results. It was a rebuke for U.S. President Donald Trump, of course. It is less clear to me what the voters want as an alternative. So I wanted to ask you, what are the top three issues you see as takeaways that the American people want from a new Congress?

Jason Crow: I actually think it is pretty clear what people want as an alternative. I sometimes get asked what our agenda should be come January. How about we do what we said we were going to do during the election? That’s the agenda—there’s no secret to this …

RA: Sure, but the reason why I phrased my question as I did is that the Democratic Party represents a pretty wide tent. You were part of building that strategy of selecting candidates for specific states and, on an even more micro level than that, for specific districts. So it is a wide tent, and not everyone agrees with each other.

JC: There is broad consensus on the core principles of this election. First, stop conflict with Iran, which is one of the biggest factors driving up costs in a reckless, lawless war that Americans don’t want. It’s one of the most bipartisan issues in America right now—Republicans and Democrats alike want the endless cycle of conflict in the Middle East to stop.

Second, stop the tariff and trade wars that are devastating farmers and ranches and businesses across this country.

Third, roll back the cuts to the Affordable Care Act subsidies, which have devastated our healthcare system, doubled and tripled many Americans’ healthcare premiums, and in 2027 are going to result in hundreds of hospital and clinic closures.

And fourth, go after corruption. This was the first anti-corruption election in my lifetime. Corruption became a kitchen-table issue. Americans saw that corruption has a direct impact on their lives and pocketbooks. They’ve sent a very clear mandate that they want us to go after corruption and to clean up their government.

RA: Right. Let’s talk more about that first factor. Trump launched that war with Iran without congressional approval. He conducted the Venezuela operation in January without informing Congress. There is gunboat diplomacy in the Caribbean, again, with Congress not able to do much to move the needle. Why couldn’t Congress do more, and what will actually change on that front come January?

JC: Congress can do more. Congress has the power. The problem is that Congress hasn’t used that power for many decades. I think it’s really important to note that this is not just a Donald Trump problem. For 25 years now, Congress has given blank checks in the form of faulty authorizations for the use of military force that aren’t clearly delineated and don’t have sunset provisions, which have allowed multiple presidents—Democratic and Republican alike—over multiple Congresses, also controlled by Democrats and Republicans alike, to continue a perpetual cycle of conflict.

The framers of the U.S. Constitution put an accountability loop in place: The people that decide when and how to go to war are the people’s representatives in Congress. We’re supposed to debate it, vote on it, let our constituents know where we stand, and then we’re supposed to fund it. That loop is broken. We’ve been debt funding it for over two decades, but we haven’t been debating and voting on it for over two decades, in many cases.

That has to end. We have the power, and that’s what we need to do in January. We have to look at the authorizations for use of military force, which we’re going to do. We’re also going to look at reforming the War Powers Act. It’s my personal belief that we should cut off funding for the Iran war and end it as quickly as we can.

RA: Critics have pointed out that it is very hard to use the power of the purse, especially when a country is already at war. Congress historically has done very little to withhold funding for wars, mostly because it will get criticized immediately. People will say you’re putting troops there in harm’s way and that you’re actively signaling to an adversary that Congress isn’t willing to do what it takes to win. How are you going to navigate that specific issue?

JC: They always say that. For 25 years, they’ve said, “We can’t pull out now. We just have to keep on throwing money at it.” Every year, we are told that we have to double down and keep going. Well, 25 years, $3 trillion, and 7,000 American lives later, after hundreds of thousands have been wounded and our credibility is in tatters, these wars ended poorly. So when somebody tells me we can’t possibly cut funding off, I say, “Actually, we can. Watch me.”

That’s different from saying that we’re going to charge the military to make sure that we wrap this up responsibly, that we’re going to do what’s called “retrograde operations,” so we protect our troops and our interests. We have the ability to do that. We have done that in the past.

I simply will not buy this argument that once we’re at war, we have to stick it out. It’s just not going to work. And Americans don’t want it. Americans know that that argument is a farce. What’s crazy is Donald Trump campaigned on this. He said he was going to end this endless cycle of conflict, and then he turned his back and doubled down on it. We have to wrap it up quickly and cut off funding.

RA: In my view, Trump basically has three options in the Iran war. One would be to escalate, even though many analysts would point out that is a terrible idea.

JC: It is a terrible idea. That’s another one of those things that has been said for 25 years. “We’re going to escalate to fix it and then to solve it.” How many times did we try that in Iraq and Afghanistan—15?

RA: Right, you served in those conflicts and know this so well.

But the second option would be to do something small quickly, declare victory, and try to get out. The third would be to actively pursue diplomacy. Of that second and third option, which one would you push for?

JC: I’d push for a combination of both. We have to make sure we’re protecting ourselves and that we’re drawing down effectively. Diplomacy is really the only way out. We can’t bomb our way to a resolution. That will never work. The Iranian regime is built to withstand that.

Our largest adversaries—Russia and China—are so happy that we are tied up in spending our stockpiles, money, and attention in Iran and not paying attention to what’s going on in the Pacific or the Russia-Ukraine conflict. They’re delighted that this is happening. So I want to pivot away from this as quickly as possible. We have the capability to do that while also protecting ourselves against a malignant Iranian regime. We have the intelligence capability. We still have the military capability to respond if we need to.

The only way out of this is to put together an international coalition of partners that will make sure we’re protecting the region, respecting navigation rights in the Strait of Hormuz, and preventing Iran from having a nuclear weapon. That’s what we did before and can continue to do.

Here’s what Congress can actually do in the next two years.

RA: The Republican Party managed to block an attempt to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth this week. What happens next here? Are you confident that a new House of Representatives will try to impeach Hegseth? And are you sure you think that is worth it?

JC: It’s my opinion that we should, and I’ve been very clear to my colleagues and to leadership about that. I have a great disdain for Hegseth, but it’s not about that for me. There are a lot of people in this business that I don’t like, but I can get over that.

For me, it’s about the fact that our 1 million-plus men and women in uniform right now, who are around the world conducting combat operations and are at risk, have a failed leader at the helm of the Department of Defense. Hegseth is not just incompetent. He is corrupt and trying to change the face and the culture of the military to match his own vision, which would be a stark departure from the historic legacy of what our military should be, which is a reflection of our country and a standard-bearer of our values. As long as he is at the perch at the Pentagon, I will do everything possible to get him removed, because our service members deserve nothing less.

RA: As we said at the start, the Democrats represent a very wide tent right now. I’m curious how you’re imagining this group will go about formulating a new foreign policy. Crucially, I want to know what areas you imagine will emerge as key differences from not only the Trump era of the last two years, but also from the years under former President Joe Biden.

JC: I think I have pretty good insight into that because, as the battleground chair for House Democrats, I visited all 12 battleground states, where I participated in countless events with farmers, doctors, nurses, and factory workers, in all sorts of communities—urban, rural, red, blue, purple.

What I can tell you is that Americans don’t want to go back. They don’t like the devastation and the chaos of this administration, but they also don’t want us to go back to where we were before. What they want us to do is move forward and to build a system that’s structured differently and that has different people at the helm that will deliver for working-class Americans.

I highlight working-class Americans because they feel as though they have been uniquely impacted by faulty trade deals, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, deindustrialization, and technology and automation, which I agree with. They want a foreign policy that’s designed to make their lives better, that delivers for them. Every decision should be focused to that end. This shouldn’t be that hard.

RA: Can I ask you to put a little bit more meat on the bone there with some specifics? Directionally, a lot of what you’re saying sounds to me like “foreign policy for the middle class,” which was the Biden administration’s slogan.

JC: I was getting to that. Working-class Americans want foreign policy focused on them, which is a very important organizing principle. This differentiates them from the middle class. This is actually really a key point: Working class is extremely different from middle class. When you refer to working-class people, you’re talking about a particular way of work, type of work, and way that a person lives their life.

In America, there is a unique culture and dignity to the working class. When you say “middle class,” that means something very different in the mind of a working-class American. That was one of the defects of Biden’s policy. Almost every American thinks of themselves as middle class. But people know when they’re working class. There’s pride there.

I’m finalizing organizing principles for what I believe the future of foreign policy should look like and what we need to be focusing on. My top principle is changing the pipeline of talent. Americans don’t trust our institutions anymore. That’s very clear. And that’s hard for some people to hear.

This is why Trump won his election and why we ended up with the Department of Government Efficiency—Americans pushed back. They want significant changes to our institutions, and they don’t see themselves reflected in them. Our foreign-policy and national security apparatus is mostly run by people who went to the same two universities and grew up within 100 miles of an ocean.

That has to change. There are 200 million Americans that live in flyover country, in the heartland. There’s tremendous talent, tremendous diversity in this nation. And we have to completely alter our talent pipeline, tap into that, and help build the next generation of leadership and civil servants and diplomats who will lead us forward.

RA: I am right in thinking here that you’re talking not just about representatives in Congress, but also about the policy incubators—the think tanks, the media, the wider ecosystem that builds the class of people who advise people like you in Congress?

JC: Exactly. That ecosystem has become very insular. It does not turn over, and it hasn’t tapped into our country. There’s very little feedback between that ecosystem and the rest of the country right now. I don’t think anyone can dispute that. Americans certainly know it’s true. There is a huge gap between what happens here in D.C. and what everyday Americans are thinking about.

That is why trust is so broken. It’s all about people. The first step has to be getting the right people on the bus to make sure that we are restoring that trust and closing that gap.

Ravi Agrawal is the editor in chief of Foreign Policy. X: @RaviReports

#6002. Dan Patrick concedes Texas ‘turned purple’ after Democrats’ historic blue wave

Outgoing Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick says in podcast that the state "turned purple" after Democrats flipped a U.S. Senate seat, captured the governor’s office and the Texas House.

Outgoing Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, a Republican, acknowledged Thursday that the Lone Star State "turned purple" after Democrats' so-called blue wave swept statewide races and flipped the governor’s office, a U.S. Senate seat and Texas House.

During his latest episode of the "Lt. Dan Podcast," Patrick acknowledged that Texas’ political makeup is shifting left but stopped short of saying the state had turned blue after many others had described it as now a blue state.

"Right now, I’d say it’s purple," he said. "We've been winning consistently, and people see it as a red state. But this time, the Democrats turned out more of their Democrat voters than Republicans turned out of their voters. But what really made the difference were the independent voters, the voters who don't vote in Republican or Democrat primaries. They only vote in general elections.

"For almost every election, we’ve been winning those voters. We didn’t win them now. Will they stay voting for Democrats in the future? Two years ago, they almost all voted for the president. Four years ago, almost all voted for [Gov.] Greg Abbott, myself and the other Republicans. So, I wouldn’t say we are a blue state, but we’ve turned purple for this moment.

TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES

Outgoing Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick acknowledged that the Lone Star State "turned purple." (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)

"The wave election, a lot of factors involved from the top down, from Washington down to Texas and all the other states where Republicans lost," Patrick added.

"I would say it's a group of voters who are willing to change their vote election to election depending on how they feel and how they feel about who's in charge. So, we're not a blue state, but we're going to have to work too hard to be sure in '28 and '30 and '32 we don't become one."

Patrick, who ran for re-election but lost his race to Democrat Vikki Goodwin, was among the Republicans hit by Democrats' blue wave. Abbott, who was vying for a fourth term, lost in his re-election bid to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, and Texas Attorney General and U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton was defeated by Democrat James Talarico as part of huge Dem gains in the state and across the country, including in other traditional GOP strongholds.

Democrats won every statewide race in Texas, bringing an end to decades of Republican control in contests that had once been considered sure bets for the GOP and leaving Sen. Ted Cruz as the only Republican holding statewide elected office.

TRUMP'S GAMBLE ON KEN PAXTON BACKFIRES AS DEMOCRAT PULLS OFF HISTORIC TEXAS SENATE UPSET

Democrats won every statewide race in Texas, bringing an end to decades of Republican control. (Jason Fochtman/Houston Chronicle, File)

Patrick said Republicans lost voters in places and demographics they had gained in 2024, including the Rio Grande Valley and young voters. He joined President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other Republican leaders in attributing the party's disastrous showing last week primarily to voters’ frustrations over affordability and the Iran war, which has caused soaring fuel prices.

Gas prices are about 83 cents per gallon higher than a year ago, according to AAA, which listed the national average at $3.91 per gallon on Thursday, compared with $3.08 a year earlier.

"We were in a tidal wave, a tsunami that washed across the country where people just said, 'I can’t afford to feed my family. I can’t afford to pay my bills. I can’t even afford to fill up my car or truck,'" Patrick said.

"It was almost to the point where, no matter what our message was, it didn’t matter. People were unhappy, and I get it."

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott lost his re-election to Democrat Gina Hinojosa and Texas Attorney General and U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton was defeated by Democrat James Talarico as part of huge Democrat gains in the state. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images, File)

"People can agree with you on cultural issues or policy issues, but it doesn’t mean they’re gonna vote for you if they can’t afford groceries," he added.

Patrick further acknowledged that the war in the Middle East has increased the cost of fuel but refused to denounce Trump's decision to attack Iran.

"I totally support the president on that. If they had intelligence that Iran was gonna get a nuclear weapon, we could be in the middle of World War III if he didn’t take action, or Israel could have already been blown off the map," Patrick said.

"So, I support what the president did, but the reality is that had an impact."

#6000. Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources said Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

In 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

“The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented,” Walker said. “Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this important position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

#5999. The Coming Era of Undersea Anarchy

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: The Coming Era of Undersea Anarchy

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.
